title: Using the workbench
intro: One editor for lesson examples, exercises and your own projects. Start with the lesson controls; open Tools when you need more inspection or project options.

sections.title: Edit, run and compare
paragraphs: Registers are the processor’s working storage. Open the addition workbench. If a saved draft differs from the example below, choose Restore starter; Undo restore recovers your draft. The first two lines load values into registers. The third adds them into t2.

Predict what t2 will hold, then choose Build & Run. Inspect the register values after the code finishes. Change a starting number in the editor, predict again, and run the edited code. Each run starts a fresh machine. Stop ends the current run.
A prediction is checked against the code you run, including your edits. A valid edit can produce a different result from the original example.

sections.title: Choose what to inspect
paragraphs: The workbench shows the registers relevant to the current example. Open Tools for further inspection, starting setup and saved projects. Choosing a tool keeps your source in the same editor.
Observations belong to the named pause or completed run. If you edit the code afterwards, build again before using the values to explain your changes.
rows: Captured integer-register values, with filters for pinned or changed registers and an optional bit view.
Observed bytes in the selected data or stack region. Before and After compare the supplied data with the captured data.
Observed bytes around sp, the stack pointer.
Breakpoints and the register or memory values you choose to watch.
Your source within the complete program, or machine instructions from the last successful build.
Your program’s console text. The addition example prints no console text.
Compiler, assembler and linker messages, plus execution errors.
Starting registers, supplied data and the highlighted result register.
Saved projects, examples, new projects and file import or export.

sections.title: Follow execution
paragraphs: Start stepping pauses before the first machine instruction of your code. Step instruction executes one machine instruction. In assembly, the execution highlight identifies the source line for the next instruction. A source line can expand into several machine instructions.

A breakpoint pauses before its instruction runs. In the addition example, choose the numbered button beside `add`, then choose Start debugging. Continue runs to the next selected breakpoint or the end of your code. Open Tools → Debugger to inspect breakpoints and watches.

C debugging uses actual instruction addresses because this compiler provides no C source-line mappings. In Tools → Program, choose Machine instructions to inspect the executable from the last successful build.

sections.title: Try an optional exercise
paragraphs: After Change it and run again, open Optional exercise. Read the task, then choose Load exercise. The editor opens your saved exercise draft, or the starter if none exists. Check all cases runs your code on fresh inputs. Return to example brings back your example draft.

sections.title: Use familiar editing controls
paragraphs: Syntax highlighting and bracket matching help you read the code. Diagnostics report whether the tools accept it.
rows: Leave the editor using the keyboard. Close Find first if it is open.

sections.title: Make room for code
paragraphs: Resize from the editor’s lower-right corner, or choose Expand editor. Full screen fills the screen; when fullscreen is unavailable, Expand workspace fills the browser window. Escape leaves fullscreen or the expanded workspace. Close Find first if it is open.

sections.title: Keep or restore your work
paragraphs: The example and optional exercise keep separate drafts. Drafts save in this browser when storage is available; check the save message. Download code keeps a source file.
Restore starter replaces your edits; Undo restore recovers them. In Tools → Program, inspect the complete source to see the supplied entry, reporting and exit code around your work.
A saved project keeps source and starting setup together. Export project saves both in one JSON file. Saved drafts and projects do not keep a running or paused machine.

sections.title: Work on an independent project
paragraphs: Use the lesson’s example and optional exercise for guided work. To keep an independent experiment, open Tools → Projects and choose Save a copy. The project opens in the same editor with its own source and starting setup.
In a lesson draft, Apply setup opens a project copy with the values you entered. The lesson draft and its starting setup stay unchanged.
A copy of an exercise uses the selected case’s inputs and data. Project edits keep the lesson draft unchanged. Choose Return to lesson to restore the example or exercise you left.
Open the playground from the course overview to work on independent projects. In a lesson, use Tools → Projects to keep working in the same editor.
